note: Every utterance below is verbatim from calls/ and events.jsonl. The naive column is the value the model extracted from the transcript; the validated column is computed live by the real validators, so it cannot drift from the code.

scenes.caller: reading a policy number that is not on file
partials: Yes, my policy number is C411.
Yes, my policy number is KD4-1188.
scenes.transcript: Yes, my policy number is KD4-1188.
scenes.why: Transcription was biased toward the list of real policy numbers, so the recognizer rewrote a wrong number into a real one. The exact-match check passed because the match had been manufactured: the validator was structurally powerless. Only reading the value back catches this.

scenes.caller: spelling a policy number letter by letter
scenes.why: Spelled-out alphanumerics are where speech recognition is weakest.

scenes.caller: reading the twin of another policy on file
partials: bravo x-ray seven, four four two zero
scenes.transcript: bravo x-ray seven, four four two zero
scenes.why: BX7-4420 and BX7-4402 are both real policies belonging to different people. The readback separates them audibly: 'four four two zero' against 'four four zero two'.

scenes.caller: giving a name one letter from the policy holder
scenes.why: The holder is Denise Holloway. One letter apart is a mishearing, not a different person, so it is worth asking rather than either accepting or refusing.

scenes.caller: giving a date with no year
scenes.why: A date without a year is not a date. Guessing the current year would silently decide whether the claim falls inside the policy period.

scenes.transcript: Someone hit my car on purpose.
scenes.naive: Someone hit my car on purpose
scenes.why: Collision and vandalism are an accident-versus-deliberate distinction that changes how the claim is handled. Two categories match, so the agent asks.
